A content delivery network, or CDN, is a system of computers spread across many cities that helps websites load quickly no matter where a visitor happens to be. Normally, every request for a photo, video, or webpage travels all the way back to the origin server — the single main computer where the website's original files live. If that server is far away, loading feels slow. A CDN fixes this by storing copies of those files in many edge locations, which are smaller computers placed closer to where people actually are, like in different countries or regions. When someone requests a page, the nearby edge location checks whether it already has a saved copy. If it does, that's called a cache hit, meaning the file was delivered instantly from nearby storage instead of the distant original server. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries holding copies of popular books, so nobody has to travel to one faraway central library every time they want to read something. This setup reduces waiting time, eases pressure on the origin server, and keeps things running smoothly even when many people request the same content at once. It also adds resilience: if one location has trouble, another nearby copy can usually step in. Without this system, popular websites would slow dramatically during busy periods, and one overloaded computer could disrupt access for everyone relying on it.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|------|----------------|-----------------|
| Origin server | The original computer storing a website's files | It's the ultimate source, but slow if used for every request |
| Edge location | A nearby computer holding copied files | Cuts travel distance, making pages load faster |
| Cache hit | A successful delivery from a saved nearby copy | Means no trip to the distant original server was needed |
| Latency | The delay before content starts appearing | Lower delay creates a smoother, faster experience |
